templates.pattern: A person has a cardiac output of [CO] L/min and a body surface area of [BSA] m². Calculate the cardiac index in L/min/m².
templates.explanation:
Cardiac index = cardiac output ÷ body surface area
= [CO] ÷ [BSA]
= [RESULT] L/min/m²

Normal cardiac index is 2.5-4.0 L/min/m². It corrects cardiac output for body size allowing fair comparison between individuals. Values below 2.2 indicate cardiogenic shock.

templates.pattern: The heart has an end-diastolic volume of [EDV] mL and an end-systolic volume of [ESV] mL. Calculate the ejection fraction as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Ejection fraction = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume × 100
= [SV] ÷ [EDV] × 100
= [RESULT]%

Normal ejection fraction is 55-70%. Values below 40% indicate heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. It is one of the most important measures of cardiac function.

templates.pattern: A patient's arterial blood has a bicarbonate concentration of [HCO3] mmol/L and a partial pressure of CO₂ of [PCO2] mmHg. Calculate the arterial pH using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. (pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO3] ÷ (0.0307 × [PCO2])))
templates.explanation:
pH = 6.1 + log₁₀(HCO₃⁻ ÷ (0.0307 × PCO₂))
= 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO3] ÷ (0.0307 × [PCO2]))
= 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO3] ÷ [0.0307*PCO2])
= 6.1 + [log10(HCO3/(0.0307*PCO2))]
= [RESULT]

The normal arterial pH is 7.35-7.45. The constant 0.0307 converts PCO₂ in mmHg to dissolved CO₂ in mmol/L. This equation is essential for interpreting acid-base disturbances such as respiratory acidosis, metabolic alkalosis and their compensations.

templates.pattern: A patient has a glomerular filtration rate of [GFR] mL/min and a renal plasma flow of [RPF] mL/min. Calculate the filtration fraction as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Filtration fraction = GFR ÷ renal plasma flow × 100
= [GFR] ÷ [RPF] × 100
= [RESULT]%

Normal filtration fraction is 15-20%. It represents the proportion of plasma filtered at the glomerulus. An elevated filtration fraction may indicate reduced renal plasma flow.

templates.pattern: A drug has a half life of [THALF] hours and an initial plasma concentration of [C0] mg/L. Calculate the plasma concentration after [TIME] hours.
templates.explanation:
Plasma concentration = C₀ × (0.5)^(t ÷ T½)
= [C0] × (0.5)^([TIME] ÷ [THALF])
= [C0] × (0.5)^[TIME/THALF]
= [RESULT] mg/L

This continuous decay formula works for any time point — not just whole half lives. It is essential for calculating drug dosing intervals in clinical pharmacology.

templates.pattern: A person has a tidal volume of [TV] mL, an anatomical dead space of [DS] mL and a breathing rate of [BR] breaths per minute. Calculate the alveolar ventilation rate in mL per minute.
templates.explanation:
Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × breathing rate
= ([TV] − [DS]) × [BR]
= [TV-DS] × [BR]
= [RESULT] mL/min

Dead space air does not participate in gas exchange. Alveolar ventilation is always less than pulmonary ventilation. Shallow rapid breathing increases dead space proportion and reduces gas exchange efficiency.

templates.pattern: Blood has an oxygen content of [OC] mL O₂/dL and a cardiac output of [CO] dL/min. Calculate the oxygen delivery to the tissues in mL O₂/min.
templates.explanation:
Oxygen delivery = cardiac output × oxygen content
= [CO] × [OC]
= [RESULT] mL O₂/min

Normal oxygen delivery is about 1000 mL/min at rest. Critically ill patients with low cardiac output or anaemia have reduced oxygen delivery — this is the main determinant of tissue oxygenation.

templates.pattern: Urine has a creatinine concentration of [U] mg/mL. Urine flow rate is [V] mL/min. Plasma creatinine concentration is [P] mg/mL. Calculate the creatinine clearance in mL/min.
templates.explanation:
Creatinine clearance = (urine creatinine × urine flow) ÷ plasma creatinine
= ([U] × [V]) ÷ [P]
= [U*V] ÷ [P]
= [RESULT] mL/min

Creatinine clearance closely approximates GFR. It is used clinically to assess kidney function and calculate drug doses in patients with renal impairment.

templates.pattern: Arterial blood has an oxygen content of [CaO2] mL O₂/dL and mixed venous blood has an oxygen content of [CvO2] mL O₂/dL. Cardiac output is [CO] dL/min. Calculate the oxygen consumption in mL O₂/min.
templates.explanation:
Oxygen consumption (VO₂) = cardiac output × (arterial O₂ content − venous O₂ content)
= [CO] × ([CaO2] − [CvO2])
= [CO] × [DIFF]
= [RESULT] mL O₂/min

This is the Fick principle. Normal VO₂ at rest is 200-300 mL/min. The arterio-venous oxygen difference reflects how much O₂ tissues extract from each dL of blood. A widening difference signals reduced cardiac output or increased tissue oxygen demand.
